articles.title: China firm gave Iran lifeline to collect Hormuz tolls before pulling plug amid US warning
articles.summary: After briefly issuing a web security certificate for a portal linked to Iran's U.S.-sanctioned Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Shanghai-based firm revoked it, though the move could still draw scrutiny under U.S. sanctions rules
articles.body: Iran’s sanctioned Persian Gulf Straits Authority (PGSA) regained secure online access for four days after a Shanghai-based internet security firm provided and then revoked its web credentials, enabling Tehran to vet vessels, collect Strait of Hormuz tolls and operate despite U.S. digital restrictions, global internet monitors said. TrustAsia issued an automated domain-validated certificate, a routine process that verifies control of a website domain through server checks and typically does not involve manual vetting or background checks. The move prompted U.S. sanctions experts, including Jeremy Paner, a partner at Hughes Hubbard & Reed, to urge TrustAsia to review its compliance program before offering further services to the IRGC-linked maritime authority — with Paner warning them to act "before it is too late." The PGSA first said its website was disrupted Aug. 10 because of "the enemy's political influence on the internet service provision systems," according to a post on X. IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE' NetBlocks CEO Alp Toker told Fox News Digital that the authority had lost its web security credentials after the entity was added to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions list on May 27. The loss of standard SSL/TLS certificates, Toker said, made the PGSA website inaccessible using standard browsers. This forced shipping firms to use unencrypted connections that, according to Toker, could leave their data vulnerable to interception. While no data breaches resulting from the use of these connections have been made known, and there are no known instances in which a shipping firm’s data was intercepted and used to its detriment because of the certificate expiration, Toker said the site’s inaccessibility resulted in a shift to what he described as "insecure protocols." "The digital transparency records are authoritative on this," he said, adding that the measure forced the traffic into a format that could be readily intercepted. "This is a class of vulnerability open to government exploitation, rather than a corporate breach or personal data leak." Toker claimed this could make it easier for authorities to read communications sent through the platform, potentially identifying shipping firms collaborating with the PGSA. TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR "The net result was that the website was more difficult to access, because most web browsers strongly encourage the use of secure HTTPS," Toker said, adding that any form submissions could have been easily "eavesdropped on because they're no longer encrypted in transit." "The mentioned issue has been resolved, and the secure domain is now once again available for submitting requests using any browser," the PGSA said six days later on Aug. 17 and in another post shared on X. "If the issue recurs in the future, the HTTP domain will again be temporarily available using the Firefox browser." Toker confirmed that Iran had turned to Shanghai-based certificate authority TrustAsia Technologies, which he said issued new digital security credentials to the PGSA despite the U.S. sanctions, restoring secure access to its website. "Iran’s IRGC extorts vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz through the so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority," the Treasury Department said in May when designating the entity, adding that the PGSA "spearheads an Iranian-controlled scheme that flagrantly violates international law and U.S. sanctions." "Anyone cooperating with the so-called strait authority may be providing support to and receiving services from the IRGC, which ultimately benefits from this attempted extortion, and may therefore be exposed to sanctions risk," the Treasury Department warned. The Chinese firm bills itself as a "leading and professionally certified certification authority in China with its focus on trusted, secure and cryptographic communications in the digital world." Its mission, it says, is to "Build trust everywhere in the digital world." "Almost all of these root authorities do business with the U.S., so they tend to comply with U.S. sanctions," Toker said. But TrustAsia, he noted, had "gone its own way, building a China-first certificate infrastructure that sidesteps the West." Toker said TrustAsia had "simply gone ahead and issued Iran's PGSA with a new certificate, and Iran was once again collecting revenue from ships passing the Strait via its secure online portal." TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS Paner warned that U.S. authorities would have enforcement powers over such actions. "The U.S. has incredibly broad authority to impose sanctions on non-Iranian companies that provide any sorts of services to sanctioned Iranian companies," he told Fox News Digital. "Many times, that authority will be abbreviated or explained as being providers of material support to sanctioned Iranian companies. But in fact, any level of services whatsoever could be the basis for the United States imposing sanctions against the company for providing services to Iran." "Restoration of the certificate is unequivocally sanctionable," Paner warned. "Restoring the certificate is/was a service provided to the PGSA, which can be the basis for imposing sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended. "That authority does not in any way require that the service be ‘knowingly’ provided to the PGSA. In other words, the automated nature of the service is irrelevant and does not make the service any less sanctionable," the lawyer added. In a statement to Fox News Digital on Aug. 20, a spokesperson for TrustAsia confirmed that the firm issued a "Domain Validated TLS certificate for pgsa.ir." "Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention," the firm said before clarifying that "DV certificates are issued through automated validation of control over the requested domain names." IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP "This process does not verify or assert the legal identity, affiliation, or sanctions status of the entity operating or benefiting from the domain. "As a result, the relationship described in your inquiry was not identified during the automated issuance process." Following the firm's review, TrustAsia said it "added the entire pgsa.ir domain namespace to our restricted-issuance list to prevent further issuance or renewal." "We also expect to complete revocation of the existing certificate within this week," the spokesman said on Aug. 20. These actions are precautionary compliance and risk-control measures. They should not be interpreted as a finding that the certificate was technically misissued, TrustAsia said. Toker confirmed the TrustAsia certificate's privilege had been withdrawn on Aug. 21 at 12:15:25 UTC. "This usually means the issuer has taken action," he said. The internet expert clarified that the revocation will gradually be coming into effect, with the firm "signaling that the PGSA certificate should no longer be trusted, and they're distributing this notice that privilege is withdrawn, usually meaning customer misuse or breached terms of use." "The secure website will stop working in most browsers, unless the owners can find a certificate authority that's willing to issue a new certificate," Toker said. IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY After reviewing TrustAsia's statement, Paner also said that OFAC would expect the company to "use the discovery as an opportunity to enhance its compliance program before it is too late." The former OFAC official clarified that Iran's revenue collection in the waterway would likely draw high-level scrutiny in Washington. "Iran's attempt to extort the world in the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz is of the utmost importance to OFAC, which is the agency that implements and enforces U.S. economic sanctions." Because major U.S. web browsers currently recognize TrustAsia’s root certificates, American systems would have automatically trusted the sanctioned Iranian portal. Toker claimed the Treasury Department could have found TrustAsia in violation of sanctions for providing material assistance to a blocked entity, potentially forcing tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to revoke trust in TrustAsia. There is no evidence that this process had begun or was likely to occur. "This could have splintered the global chain of trust and potentially render much of the Chinese web inaccessible from the West," Toker warned. IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT Paner clarified that the certificates authenticate the site, boosting its credibility, and suggested TrustAsia should have weighed the risks of working with sanctioned entities. "There's always reputational risk involved in any company that decides to do business with the IRGC." "If I were advising TrustAsia, I would at minimum immediately identify all other IRGC companies receiving services." Paner added that this latest situation aligned with broader warnings from administration officials. "I think this dovetails pretty nicely with Secretary Bessent's comments about how the coming sanctions are going to be unlike any that has come prior. Sanctions require a careful balancing of the costs and the benefits. "When it's a Chinese tech company providing necessary services to the IRGC, I'm confident that the U.S. government is going to forego any sort of balancing in that regard." The United States on Aug. 24 had sanctioned nearly 60 Iran-linked individuals, entities and vessels and expanded the threat of secondary sanctions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. These did not include TrustAsia. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Bessent described the measures as part of an "economic onslaught" targeting Tehran’s global financial networks under "Operation Economic Outcast." A Chinese Embassy spokesperson also said in a statement: "I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned. I have no information to provide." Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the White House for comment.

articles.title: From Macaca to MAGA: How one needling remark can become a political thorn for Donald Trump
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondant from Washington: Twenty years ago, a single word helped change the balance of power in Washington.In 2006, Republican Senator George.
articles.body: TOI correspondant from Washington: Twenty years ago, a single word helped change the balance of power in Washington.In 2006, Republican Senator George Allen of Virginia was cruising toward re-election and was being talked about as a possible presidential candidate.Then, at a campaign rally, he pointed to S R Sidarth, a young Indian-American volunteer tracking his campaign for Democrat Jim Webb, and called him “Macaca” (monkey), before adding, “Welcome to America and the real world of Virginia.”The episode went viral, by the modest standards of the pre-TikTok, pre-X era, and transformed the Virginia Senate race. Allen's once-comfortable lead evaporated, and Webb eventually won by just 9,329 votes, giving Democrats the 51st seat they needed to take control of the Senate.Contemporary polling showed Allen's lead shrinking dramatically after the incident in a state with a significant Indian-American population adjoining Washington DC.The lesson was not that one offensive comment single-handedly decides an election (Allen was decidedly pro-India). It was that stray remarks and small events can have large consequences when voters are already paying attention.A seemingly inconsequential slight can become a symbol, particularly when it resonates with a community, in this case Indian-Americans, that feels it has been singled out, which is what appears to be happening in Texas.Karl Rove, the legendary Republican strategist who helped George Bush win the White House in 2000, says he will now do something he has done only once before in his life: vote for a Democrat.The immediate trigger was a social-media post last week by Republican candidate Bo French after a football game showing mostly Indian-origin students celebrating in the stands. Compounding his inflammatory rhetoric about race, religion, immigration and minorities, French suggested that the photo showed Americans had been “displaced by foreigners”, brown-skinned Indians.“These people are diminishing the Republican Party, not building it. I’ll have no part of it,” Rove wrote in oped on Friday, referring to French and his incendiary posts and comments. Other moderate Republicans, notably Senator John Cornyn, ousted by Trump, have also condemned French’s post that became a lightning rod for anti-Indian campaign among MAGA hardliners.All this is happening when the Republican relationship with Trump is acquiring something resembling buyer's remorse.There was a time when GOP candidates would have walked through fire for a photograph with the MAGA boss. Now, with the midterm elections weeks away, some appear reluctant even to walk into the same room.Among them is Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican and former Trump champion among Hispanic voters. In a campaign advertisement released this week, she told Trump that his immigration enforcement had “gone too far” and warned that Hispanics who helped return him to the White House in 2024 “feel betrayed.”Then there’s podcaster Joe Rogan, whose significance is not simply that he is another celebrity with a microphone. His podcast reaches an enormous audience and, in 2024, he endorsed Trump after interviewing him for nearly three hours, serving as an important bridge between Trump and younger male voters who had not traditionally been reliable Republican voters.This week, however, Rogan unloaded on some Trump supporters after they attacked comedian Jelly Roll over jokes about Trump. “Trump supporters are f***ing nuts, man,” Rogan said.“They’re rabid.” More and more Trump supporters are starting to distance themselves from the President even as commentators are finding new ways to say that he's basically unhinged.None of this makes a Democratic takeover of Congress inevitable. But if Democrats were to win both chambers, as some polls are suggesting, Trump's presidency would continue; what would change is his political operating environment, with greater congressional scrutiny, tougher confirmation fights and more contested battles over spending, trade, sanctions, arms and military policy.For foreign governments, that distinction matters. It could throw up a Congress much less willing to provide the president a blank cheque. Trump built his political career on the proposition that Republicans needed more Trump to win.The 2026 campaign is beginning to test that. As George Allen discovered two decades ago, campaigns sometimes learn the hard way that a small slight – or a scabrous social media post – can become a thorn that can cost the party the Senate.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Poland joins coalition to strengthen Ukraine’s air defences against Russia
articles.summary: International News: Poland has joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday, as Kyiv seeks t.
articles.body: Poland has joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday, as Kyiv seeks to strengthen its air defences against Russian attacks.“From today, Poland is part of this major project ... we agreed on the forms and frameworks of this cooperation,” Tusk said in a video posted on X.Tusk made the announcement during a summit of eight Carpathian countries being held in western Ukraine and launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Poland backs joint missile defence projectUkraine and nine European countries announced an air-defence coalition in July that would include the joint development of a new anti-ballistic missile system. The proposed system is intended to provide an alternative and cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.Tusk also said Poland had prepared a new “significant” donation package for Ukraine, although he did not provide details.“I will be very consistent here. No one will change my opinion that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression ... History cannot divide us vis-a-vis Russia today,” Tusk said.Following a bilateral meeting with Tusk at the summit, Zelenskyy thanked Poland for the new aid package.“Ukraine and Poland are strong neighbors, friends, and partners, and we have one common enemy,” he said on social media.Carpathian summit focuses on security, cooperationThe announcement came during the first Carpathian Summit in western Ukraine, which brought together Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary, with the European Union also involved.Zelenskyy said the meeting would focus on security, energy, logistics, cross-border economic ties and support for local communities.Business representatives were also expected to participate in discussions on economic cooperation, security and logistics, as Russia targets Ukraine's transport routes, according to news agency AFP.“The Carpathian macro-region has become one of the most reliable foundations of our defense. This is about strength that exists and will continue to exist,” Zelenskyy said.The summit comes as Ukraine seeks additional missile defence systems to counter Russian ballistic attacks, while also developing interceptors to tackle Russian jet-powered drones.Tusk had said before travelling to Ukraine that “Difficult weeks and months lie ahead for all of us, not just Ukraine. And it's worth showing solidarity at a time like this.”The meeting was held in the western Ukrainian ski resort of Bukovel amid growing concern among European countries over Russian hybrid threats, including sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and potential drone incursions into Nato territory.

articles.title: ‘I had no doubts’: Lone holdout juror says Lindsay Clancy deliberately killed her 3 children
articles.summary: US News: The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has said he had “no doubts” that the Massachusetts mother was criminally responsible for kil.
articles.body: The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has said he had “no doubts” that the Massachusetts mother was criminally responsible for killing her three children, despite the jury remaining deadlocked and forcing a mistrial.According to the BBC, juror Michael P Desronvil said the physical evidence, key witnesses and prosecution's case convinced him that Clancy knew what she was doing and had planned the killings. “I didn’t have any doubts,” he said in a statement issued through his lawyer.A Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial on September 4 after the 12-member jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberations. Eleven jurors ultimately supported finding Clancy not criminally responsible, while Desronvil remained the sole holdout.Clancy, 36, was accused of killing her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, at the family’s Massachusetts home on January 24, 2023. She later jumped from a second-floor window.What did the holdout juror say?Desronvil said the evidence presented during the trial was enough to establish that Clancy had intentionally killed her children and had planned the act.“As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented,” he said.His comments contrast with statements from other jurors, who have described lengthy efforts to persuade him to change his position. One juror told CBS that the panel spent several days trying to convince Desronvil after the jury became divided.Another juror told NBC that Desronvil had acknowledged reasonable doubt but still refused to support a finding that Clancy was not criminally responsible.Defence argued postpartum psychosisClancy’s defence argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children and was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong.A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a “command hallucination” and a “delusion of influence” during the killings. Prosecutors, however, argued that Clancy was aware of her actions and had planned the murders.The jury had several options, including first-degree murder, lesser charges such as manslaughter, and a finding of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.What happens next?The mistrial leaves the case unresolved, with prosecutors yet to announce whether they will seek a retrial. Clancy’s lawyer Kevin Reddington has filed a motion seeking to have the charges dropped and said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid another trial.The next court hearing is scheduled for September 29 at Plymouth Superior Court.Clancy’s former husband, Patrick Clancy, is also due to speak publicly about the case in an upcoming 60 Minutes interview, where he is expected to discuss his grief, memories of his children and conspiracy theories that circulated online after the killings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Very British Cult: Three men lose appeal for harrassing BBC journalist over documentary
articles.summary: Kristofer Deichler, Jatinder Kamra and Sukhraj Singh were given community service and restraining orders for their harassment of Catrin Nye.
articles.body:
Three men have lost their appeal for harassing BBC journalist Catrin Nye, who presented the podcast series and documentary, A Very British Cult.

Kristofer Deichler, 47, Jatinder Kamra, 46 and Sukhraj Singh, were sentenced for harassment after visiting her home where she lived with her partner and children, first in a group in August 2024, and then again as the three of them in September 2024.

"We accept she was terrified by the unexpected attendance" at her home, said Judge Pounder at Snaresbrook Crown Court, adding there was "heightened concern" as her children were also home.

All three men are members of Lighthouse, which was investigated for the 2023 documentary and podcast fronted by Nye.

Three men sentenced for harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary

Three men guilty of harassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary

The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years.

They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade.

A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC.

"While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said.

After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered.

The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping.

"The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder.

"What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable.

During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours.

The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism".

"They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained.

"That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster."

The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said.

Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested.

The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest.

Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return".

Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property.

It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said.

Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard.

The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs.

Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address".

The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC.

On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional £1,000.

articles.title: Bristol spends £9.7 million on 400m Harbour Walkway, planned for £2.5 million to link Temple Meads to an arena now moved to Filton; it instead connects the station to Bristol’s £500 million campus
articles.summary: UK News: A floating walkway that was originally conceived to take visitors from one of Bristol’s busiest railway stations to a major new music arena has finall.
articles.body: A floating walkway that was originally conceived to take visitors from one of Bristol’s busiest railway stations to a major new music arena has finally opened, but the arena it was designed to connect to will now be built around six miles away.The Harbour Walkway, which stretches for 400 metres, was initially expected to cost around £2.5 million when it was proposed in 2015. Bristol City Council has ultimately spent £9.7 million on the project, according to SWNS.The walkway opened earlier this month and is now being positioned as part of the wider redevelopment around Bristol Temple Meads and the new University of Bristol campus.From £2.5 million plan to £9.7 million projectThe original idea was relatively straightforward: create a pedestrian and cycling route linking Temple Meads station with a planned 12,000-capacity Bristol Arena.But the arena project became embroiled in delays, rising costs and disagreements over its location. Plans for a venue at Temple Meads were eventually abandoned, with the proposed arena moved to the Filton airfield site.The new venue is planned to accommodate 17,000 people, but construction has yet to begin.By then, however, work on the Harbour Walkway was already progressing.The structure was built using floating pontoons manufactured in Spain, contributing to a project that eventually cost almost four times its original £2.5 million estimate.What does the walkway connect now?Instead of leading concert-goers directly to an arena, the walkway now links the new eastern entrance of Bristol Temple Meads with the University of Bristol’s new £500 million campus.It also connects pedestrians and cyclists to Valentine Bridge, providing a crossing point over the river.The walkway starts near the ferry stop between Valentine Bridge and Meads Reach Bridge, passes underneath the railway tracks and ends at Cattle Market Road.Bristol City Council says the project is intended to improve pedestrian and cycling connections as part of the wider Temple Quarter regeneration scheme.‘£10 million is wild’: Social media reactsThe project's final price tag has triggered plenty of criticism online, particularly because its original purpose was linked to an arena that is no longer being built at Temple Meads.One commenter described it as “one of the most ridiculous pieces of construction in Bristol and potentially British history”.Another questioned whether the money could instead have been spent repairing existing pavements and walkways.One social media user wrote, “10m? And it leads to an arena that doesn’t exist? Ok.”Another said the walkway looked like “a temporary structure” and questioned what problem it was intended to solve.The cost works out at roughly £24,250 per metre based on the £9.7 million figure and the walkway’s 400-metre length.Not everyone thinks it is money wastedThe walkway has also received support from some residents.One commenter called it “lush”, while another welcomed the improved connectivity in the area.“Great to see South East Bristol getting better connected,” one person wrote.Another argued that £10 million could represent reasonable value for a public infrastructure project.The project is now part of the wider Temple Quarter regeneration, an extensive redevelopment programme involving new homes, public spaces, transport improvements and the University of Bristol’s new campus.The arena that changed locationThe story of the walkway is closely linked to Bristol’s long-running arena plans.In 2012, the council proposed a £92.5 million arena at Temple Meads. Plans for a 12,000-capacity venue were approved in 2014, but the project subsequently faced delays and disputes.Former mayor Marvin Rees later began negotiations with Malaysian-owned construction company YTL to relocate the arena to Filton.The new 17,000-capacity venue was subsequently approved by Bristol City Council. Construction is yet to begin, although work on a railway station intended to serve the future arena is under way.Meanwhile, the Harbour Walkway, originally designed with the Temple Meads arena in mind, is now open and serving a different purpose as part of Bristol’s ongoing regeneration.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
articles.summary: O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless" and said "it won't happen again".
articles.body:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".

He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments.

O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.

Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.

O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".

He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate.

"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added.

Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".

In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair".

"I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors.

"I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors."

O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again".

"I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future."

Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.

She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".

She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise.

"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.

In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."

He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".

It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business .

In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists" in a row over airport charges.

He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".

In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

articles.title: UN report finds widespread sexual violence in Ukraine war, 89% of cases linked to Russia
articles.summary: Europe News: Russian forces committed widespread sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war in Ukraine, including gang rape, genital mutilation and ele.
articles.body: Russian forces committed widespread sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war in Ukraine, including gang rape, genital mutilation and electric shocks to the genitals, while Ukrainian authorities were also responsible for a smaller number of violations, according to a UN human rights report released on Friday.The report by the UN human rights office documented 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and July 2026.Of these cases, 89% were attributed to the Russian side, including members of its armed forces, prison service and security agencies, while 11% were linked to Ukrainian authorities, including members of the Ukrainian armed forces, according to Reuters.Russia's permanent diplomatic mission in Geneva declined to comment on the report.Russian forces accused of abuse in detentionThe report said Russian authorities committed sexual violence against Ukrainian prisoners of war and civilian detainees in occupied areas of Ukraine and inside Russia at various stages of captivity, including during capture, transfer, interrogation and detention.The documented violations included gang rape, rape, genital mutilation and electric shocks to men's genitals using a Soviet-era field telephone known as a “tapik”.The findings were based on interviews with victims of sexual violence committed by both sides. The UN cautioned that the figures were not comprehensive because conflict-related sexual violence remains significantly under-reported.The report also said Russia's refusal to give the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights access to occupied Ukrainian territory, prisoners of war and civilian detainees meant the actual scale of violations was likely higher.Most victims in detention were men, particularly prisoners of war and detainees, although women and children were also affected, mainly in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.“Sexual violence in conflict is often misunderstood to be mainly affecting women and girls, where in the Ukraine war context, the majority of survivors are men,” Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said.“And men and women require different solutions and approaches to their recovery,” she added.Ukraine also accused of violationsThe report documented a smaller number of cases involving Ukrainian authorities. In Ukrainian government-controlled territory, nearly half of the violations attributed to Ukrainian authorities against Russian and third-country prisoners of war and detainees involved threats of sexual violence and beatings to the genitals.OHCHR said it did not document any cases of rape of Russian prisoners of war by Ukrainian forces.Russian and third-country prisoners of war reported sexual violence in 10 official detention facilities and 55 unofficial or transit locations, the report said.Ukraine's foreign ministry welcomed the report, saying it demonstrated the scale of human rights violations perpetrated by Russia as well as measures being taken by Kyiv to prevent such violence and compensate victims. The ministry did not directly address the findings concerning abuse by Ukrainian forces.The report said Ukraine had taken some steps to prevent such violations and had cooperated with OHCHR requests, although efforts to ensure accountability remained limited.By contrast, it said Russia had failed to take steps to prevent, investigate or prosecute sexual violence committed by its personnel and had not engaged with OHCHR requests for information.“I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine,” UN high commissioner for human rights Volker Turk said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2002, concrete rubble from Baltimore’s demolished Memorial Stadium was reused in a Maryland living shoreline; the project restored 400 feet of coast and created two acres of tidal wetlands
articles.summary: US News: Tons of crushed concrete from Baltimore’s former Memorial Stadium are getting a second life as the foundation for a growing coastal ecosystem along th.
articles.body: Tons of crushed concrete from Baltimore’s former Memorial Stadium are getting a second life as the foundation for a growing coastal ecosystem along the Chesapeake Bay. In 2002, environmental engineers placed thousands of cubic yards of clean stadium rubble along the shores of Queen Anne’s County to fight serious wave erosion. More than 20 years later, monitoring shows that the recycled stadium material has helped create two acres of healthy intertidal wetlands and restored more than 400 linear feet of shoreline. The project is part of a larger restoration effort led by the Chesapeake Bay Environmental Centre (CBEC) in Grasonville, working with the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR).Turning sports history into coastal protectionMemorial Stadium was once home to Major League Baseball’s Baltimore Orioles and the National Football League’s Baltimore Colts before it was demolished in 2001. Instead of sending all the concrete and masonry from the stadium to landfills, state planners reused much of the material for coastal projects. Workers moved clean concrete pieces, with rebar and harmful finishes removed, across the Chesapeake Bay. The material was used to build offshore breakwaters and low barriers called sills. Unlike tall wooden bulkheads or concrete seawalls, which can reflect wave energy and increase erosion, the rubble was placed in low structures. These barriers reduce the force of incoming waves while still allowing water, sediment and marine life to move between the open bay and the protected marsh.Building a living laboratoryAccording to project information from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, the state’s Watershed and Climate Service has worked with the Chesapeake Bay Environmental Centre to maintain the site as a living laboratory for coastal research. Engineers placed clean sand behind the recycled stadium sills and planted native marsh grasses, including smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora) and saltmeadow cordgrass (Spartina patens). As the plants grew, their large root systems trapped sediment carried by the water. This slowly raised the marsh surface and helped it keep up with rising sea levels.Research from the Chesapeake Bay Environmental Centre shows that living shorelines can provide several important environmental benefits compared with hard seawalls:Habitat creation: The shallow intertidal area provides nursery habitat for young blue crabs, striped bass and other small fish.Nutrient filtering: Native marsh grasses capture nitrogen and phosphorus from runoff before these pollutants reach deeper parts of the bay.Erosion control: The plants and low sills reduce the force of storm waves, helping prevent shoreline loss without increasing erosion on nearby properties.Reusing concrete to build artificial reefsThe old stadium material has also been used beyond shoreline protection. According to reports from the Maryland Artificial Reef Coalition (MARC) and the Maryland DNR Fisheries Service, crushed Memorial Stadium concrete was transported by barge to approved artificial reef locations across the bay. Placed on areas of hard seafloor, the rough concrete provides surfaces where organisms such as eastern oysters, barnacles and mussels can attach and grow. These reef structures then attract popular sportfish, including black sea bass, tautog and summer flounder. By combining offshore artificial reefs with living shorelines near the coast, marine scientists have created connected habitats that can support aquatic animals at different stages of their lives.Growing use of nature-based coastal protectionMaryland lawmakers passed the Living Shorelines Protection Act in 2008. The law made nature-based designs the standard requirement for waterfront property owners seeking permits to control erosion along state waterways. Early projects such as the Memorial Stadium site helped show property owners and contractors that softer, nature-based engineering methods could work. Today, state climate programs continue to support living shorelines as a way to protect coastal communities from stronger storms and rising sea levels. DNR field data shows that sites using strong sills and native plants have remained stable through major storms, including Hurricane Sandy and Tropical Storm Lee. Traditional bulkheads on nearby properties, meanwhile, often experienced structural damage. Monitoring at the Grasonville site continues to provide long-term information about how recycled concrete sills respond to sediment buildup, marsh growth and changing water conditions across the Mid-Atlantic.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
